setup.zh: 十月十三。你断着一根肋骨，怀里揣着舅舅的信：「你爹如今天天进黑松岭……膝盖比去年重了。」柴房里，饭桶。
setup.en: The thirteenth of the tenth month. A rib is broken, and in your coat is your uncle's letter: "Your father goes into the Heisong Ridge every day now… his knee is worse than last year." In the woodshed: Rice Bucket.

recap.zh: 开饭桶：你手边有什么扔什么——柴火棍、窝头、鞋底、牛骨头，末了两块灵石——开出一地破烂、一罐牛脂甘露，两块灵石换来一颗好看的含笑半步颠和一颗难看的解药——你当仙丹吞了好看的，笑着栽了两跤，又吞了解药；银月一根尾巴毛开出一张踏马符，符角一行小字「足下一踏，马上便走」，你不知何用，收进腰带夹层；破烂堆里滚出一颗九道金纹的回春丹。你没吃，装进辣椒油瓶，留给爹的膝盖；断着一根肋骨巡了半个月的夜——白天药园归阿禾，酉时交班，两个人的数没差过一株。马小宝把一株紫玉参栽进小狰的窝，阿禾拿本子上的数对上巡夜簿上他自己写的「陪巡」，又递了他一个台阶：「送错了窝。」月底盘账，褚先生按出那根骨头：「这根骨头，还断着。」
recap.en: Feeding Rice Bucket: you threw in whatever was to hand — firewood, a corn bun, a sandal sole, a soup bone, and last your two spirit stones — and out came a floor of junk, a pot of Beef-Tallow Sweet Dew, and for the two spirit stones a pretty Smiling Half-Step Topple and an ugly antidote — you swallowed the pretty one for an immortal's pill, grinned and went over twice, then swallowed the cure; one of Silver Moon's hairs brought out a Hoof-It Charm — *one stamp underfoot, and off at once*, said the small print — that you couldn't make sense of, tucked into your belt pocket; and out of the junk rolled one spring-return pill with nine gold lines. You didn't eat it; you put it in a chilli-oil bottle, kept for your father's knee, and walked the night watch half a month on a broken rib — the garden Ah He's by day, the count handed over at dusk, never one plant out. Ma Xiaobao planted a purple jade ginseng in Little Zheng's nest; Ah He set her daily count against the "kept watch with him" he had written in the watch book himself, then handed him a way down: "the wrong nest." At the month-end reckoning Master Chu found the bone: "This bone is still broken."

zh: 柴火棍、窝头、牛骨头，一样一样扔进去。
破烂底下，一颗。九道纹。金的。
en: Firewood, a corn bun, a soup bone — in they go, one by one.
Under the junk, one. Nine rings. Gold.

story.zh:
门外「笃笃笃」三声。他手忙脚乱，一把将小狰捞过来，往炉子上一放。小狰正睡得迷糊，四只爪子一抱，把炉子搂在肚皮底下，五条尾巴往上一盖，只露出一个红毛团子。小满把门拉得大开，自己往门框上一靠，身子把屋里挡了一半。

是周衡。他抱着账簿，看了看小满肿得只剩一条缝的左眼，看了看他捂着肋骨的那只手，道：「马师弟一早来过执事房。说你摔坏了，起不来，药园这几夜，他替你巡。」又道，「我去园门口看了巡夜簿。昨夜那一格，有一个手印。」他没说那手印是什么颜色。小满道：「是我按的。今夜，我也巡。」周衡道：「你这个样子。」小满道：「巡得了。」周衡把账簿一合：「月底盘账，只认账，不认脸。」说罢，抱着账簿走了。

小满想了很久，才想明白：昨天夜里的事，周衡知道；周衡也只认他那本账。

他把门闩上，从小狰肚皮底下把饭桶抠了出来。喂它，它吐东西——银月就留下这么一句。他盯着那只铜肚子，肋骨也忘了疼，跟小时候盯着爹从县城捎回来的拨浪鼓一个样。

头一样，扔了根柴火棍。「咯嘣」，他手心一凉，丹田里的暖给吸走一口；「咔哒」，吐出一根牙签。他来了劲：石子、半个窝头、一根黄芪的残株、一片枯叶、一根伙房熬汤剩下的牛骨头，一样一样往里扔。扔一样，吸一口，吐一样，吐的全是破烂。扔到草鞋底，它打个嗝，原样吐回来，糊了他一脸。末了他把怀里剩的两块灵石——九月那两块，早叫他这只漏勺一口一口吸干了；这两块是十月初一交完公中剩下的，离冬月初一领新的还有半个多月——也扔了进去，它「咯嘣咯嘣」嚼得山响——这才是一口正经饭。

等他回过神来，丹田早见了底，眼前一黑，额头「咚」地磕在盖子上。

地上已摆了一溜：一粒更小的石子，一块能砸核桃的锅巴，一只小陶罐——揭开是一股牛油花椒味，罐上歪歪扭扭四个字：牛脂甘露，底下一行小字：麻辣鲜香。小狰舔了一口，辣得满屋子转圈。当中还有两颗丹。一颗灰里透红，没有纹，皱巴巴的，闻着发苦，裹着一角焦黄的草纸，缩在锅巴边上，像一颗没人要的枣核。另一颗，小满一眼看过去，眼睛便挪不开了：桂圆大小，通体莹白，白里透着一层淡淡的霞光，托在一方小红纸上，自己便亮着，像庙里菩萨手上托的那一颗；红纸上有几个小字，他没顾上看；一股香气直往鼻子里钻，甜丝丝、凉丝丝的，像吴婆婆讲过的蟠桃。小狰鼻子一抽，口水「哗」地挂下来一尺长，爪子已经伸了过去。

仙丹。饭桶开出仙丹来了。

小满比狰快，一把抢在手里，想也没想，往嘴里一丢。

那丹入口便化了，甜，甜得他咧开了嘴。这一咧，就收不回去了。他想站起来，到窗口亮处瞧瞧自己身上冒没冒仙气，才迈了半步，膝盖一软，「扑通」栽进柴堆里，脸还笑着；爬起来，又迈半步，又是一跤。

一个尖鼻子探出衣领。银月的声音困得发黏，鼻子抽了两抽，一下子醒了：「……哪来的毒药？」

小满趴在柴堆里，笑得合不拢嘴：「……毒药？」

「对啊。」她瞧瞧他，又瞧瞧口水挂了一尺长的小狰，拿爪子把柴堆上那方小红纸拨了过来，念道：「含笑半步颠。」底下一行小字，她也念了：「服之开颜，步步生花。」顿了一顿，「生花？生跤。就是你这样。」她拿鼻子拱了拱锅巴边上那颗皱巴巴的，草纸上三个字：止笑丸，底下一行小字：苦海回头。「吃了。它的解药。一毒一解，一锅出的。」又道：「好看的是毒，难看的是解。记住了。」

小满笑着把那颗灰的塞进嘴里，苦得一张笑脸皱成了一团。过了一盏茶，嘴角才肯放下来。

银月瞧了一眼满地破烂，眼睛忽然直了，「嗖」地扑到那只小陶罐上，抱着罐子拿鼻子拱：「……牛油，花椒，八角——这是火锅底料！本王最爱！」她两只前爪举过头顶，「今晚火锅——耶～～」

小满瞪大了眼睛，看看她，看看罐子，又看看饭桶，一副不敢相信的样子。半晌，他慢吞吞地道：「……还不是你给的那口火锅里蹦出来的。它不该叫饭桶，该叫火锅才对。晚上就拿它涮锅吧，肯定不错。」说完，嘴角还挂着方才那点笑，两眼发直——那样子，像是受了天大的刺激，一下子傻了。

银月凑过去，拿爪子在他眼前晃了晃：「喂。解药你是不是只吃了半颗？哈哈哈哈！」

她抱着罐子不撒手，瞧了瞧满地破烂，又瞧了瞧饭桶：「看好了。本王给你开个张。」她从尾巴尖上拔下一根银毛，疼得龇了一龇牙，丢进饭桶。盖上那只小兽睁开一只眼睛，瞧了瞧她，把屁股扭过来对着她。「咔哒」，飘出一张黄纸：朱砂画的一匹马，脑袋大，身子小，四条腿像四根筷子插在一个馒头上，四只蹄子底下各点一个圈，尾巴一道弯钩勾到纸边。朱砂还是湿的，笔画里像有一丝极细的光，顺着马腿往下溜，溜进蹄子底下那四个圈里，便没了。小满憋了半天，憋出一句：「……这踏马的，是什么符？」话音才落，他瞧见符角上一行米粒大的朱字：踏马符。底下还有一行，更小：足下一踏，马上便走。

银月脸上的毛都嫌弃得竖了起来：「本王的一根毛，就换这个。『马上便走』——走哪儿去？画成这个样子，还不如本王给你画。」爪子一缩，又睡过去了。那条尾巴又暗下去一截。它不吃白饭，摸它一下，便要吃人一口。

那道符，「足下一踏」——是贴在脚底下，还是踩在脚底下？踏了，又走到哪儿去？他想不明白；一张废纸，可那是她一根尾巴毛换的，扔了舍不得。他叠成一个小方块，塞进腰带里头的夹层——娘缝来装铜钱的，一回也没装过钱。

他把一地破烂往柴垛底下塞，塞到最后，锅巴底下滚出一颗丹来，碧绿碧绿，透亮得像一滴凝住了的露水。丹身上有纹，他数了一遍，又数了一遍：九道，全是金的，一道挨着一道，像一个人一圈一圈地系着腰带；纹缝里刻着两个米粒大的字：回春。他凑近了闻，一股豆腥气，回口一点甜——是那根黄芪的残株换的。

他知道一道纹是什么样子：舅舅说过，济世堂柜台上的琉璃罐子里也摆着回春丹，暗沉沉的，一道纹，几个黑点，一颗要五两银子。他手里这一颗，九道。
story.en:
*Tock tock tock* at the door. In a flurry he grabbed Little Zheng and plonked it on the furnace. Little Zheng, half asleep, hugged the furnace under its belly with all four paws and laid its five tails over the top, so only a red ball of fur showed. Xiaoman pulled the door wide open, leaned on the frame, and blocked half the room with his body.

It was Zhou Heng. Holding his ledger, he looked at Xiaoman's left eye swollen to a slit, at the hand holding his ribs. "Brother Ma came to the stewards' office first thing. Says you had a bad fall and can't get up, and he'll watch the herb garden for you these next few nights." Then: "I went and looked at the watch book by the garden gate. Last night's box has a handprint in it." He didn't say what colour the handprint was. Xiaoman said, "I made it. Tonight I'll watch too." Zhou Heng said, "In this state." Xiaoman said, "I can watch." Zhou Heng shut the ledger. "Month-end accounts: I go by the books, not by faces." And he went off with the ledger.

It took Xiaoman a long time to understand: Zhou Heng knew what had happened last night; and Zhou Heng went only by his books.

He barred the door and dug Rice Bucket out from under Little Zheng's belly. Feed it, and it spits something out — that was all Silver Moon had left him. He stared at the bronze belly and forgot his rib, the way he had once stared at the rattle-drum his father brought home from the county town.

First he threw in a stick of firewood. *Crack* — his palms went cold, and a mouthful of the warmth in his belly was drawn away; *click* — out came a toothpick. Now he was hooked: a pebble, half a corn bun, a spent astragalus stalk from the herb garden, a dead leaf, a beef bone left over from the kitchen's soup, in they went one by one. One thing in, one draw, one thing out, and every one of them junk. When he got to a straw-sandal sole it burped and spat it straight back, all over his face. Last of all he threw in the two spirit stones he had left — September's two that leaky ladle of his had long since sipped dry; these were what remained after the first-of-October levy, with the next handout half a month off — and it crunched them *crack, crack* with great relish — now this was a proper meal.

By the time he came to himself his belly was scraped dry; his sight went black, and his forehead hit the lid with a *thunk*.

A row of things lay on the floor: an even smaller pebble, a rice crust hard enough to crack walnuts, a little clay pot — lift the lid and out came beef tallow and Sichuan pepper, with four crooked characters on the side: Beef-Tallow Sweet Dew, and under them a line of small ones: *Hot, numbing, fragrant.* Little Zheng licked it once and spun round the room in a fit of heat. Among them lay two pills as well. One was grey shot through with red, no lines, shrivelled, smelling bitter, wrapped in a scrap of scorched straw paper, huddled by the rice crust like a date stone nobody wanted. The other — Xiaoman looked once and couldn't look away: the size of a longan, white all through, a faint rosy glow beneath the white, shining by itself where it sat on a square of red paper, like the pearl the Bodhisattva holds up in her palm at the temple — there was small writing on the red paper, which he never stopped to read; and a scent that went straight up his nose, sweet and cool, like the peaches of immortality Granny Wu used to tell of. Little Zheng's nose twitched, a foot of drool came down in one *slosh*, and its paw was already reaching.

An immortal's pill. Rice Bucket had spat out an immortal's pill.

Xiaoman was quicker than the zheng: he snatched it up and, without a thought, tossed it into his mouth.

It melted on his tongue — sweet, so sweet his mouth spread into a grin. And once the grin was out, it wouldn't go back. He meant to get up and look himself over in the light by the window, to see whether he was giving off immortal vapour; he took half a step, his knees went, and *thump* — into the woodpile, face still smiling. Up again, half a step, down again.

A pointed nose came out at his collar. Silver Moon's voice was sticky with sleep; her nose twitched twice and she was wide awake: "…Where did you get poison?"

Xiaoman, sprawled in the woodpile, grinning ear to ear: "…Poison?"

"Yes." She looked at him, then at Little Zheng with a foot of drool hanging, and hooked the square of red paper over with a claw. "*Smiling Half-Step Topple.*" There was a line of small writing under it, and she read that too: "*Take it and smile; flowers at every step.*" A pause. "Flowers? Falls. Like you." She nosed the shrivelled one by the crust; three characters on its straw paper — *Laugh-Stopper Pill* — and a line of small ones: *Turn back from the bitter sea.* "Eat it. Its cure. One poison, one cure, out of the same pot." Then: "The pretty one's the poison; the ugly one's the cure. Remember that."

Still grinning, Xiaoman put the grey one in his mouth, and the bitterness screwed his smiling face into a knot. It took a cup of tea's time for the corners of his mouth to come down.

Silver Moon glanced over the floor full of junk — and her eyes went wide. Whoosh: she was on the little clay jar, hugging it, nosing at it. "…Beef tallow, peppercorn, star anise — it's hotpot base! My favourite!" Both forepaws went up over her head. "Hotpot tonight — yeah~~"

Xiaoman's eyes went wide. He looked at her, at the jar, at the rice-bucket, as if he couldn't believe any of it. At last, slowly: "…It jumped out of that hotpot you gave me. It shouldn't be called the rice-bucket — it should be called the hotpot. Let's cook in it tonight. Bound to be good." The smile from before still hung at the corner of his mouth and his eyes had gone glassy — he looked like a boy who'd had one shock too many and gone simple.

Silver Moon leaned in and waved a paw in front of his eyes. "Hey. Did you only eat half the cure? Hahahaha!"

Still hugging the jar, she looked over the junk, then at the rice-bucket. "Watch. I'll open the shop for you." She plucked a single silver hair from the tip of her tail, baring her teeth at the sting, and dropped it into Rice Bucket. The little beast on the lid opened one eye, looked at her, and turned its backside to her. *Click* — out floated a sheet of yellow paper: a horse in cinnabar, big head, small body, four legs like four chopsticks stuck in a steamed bun, a little circle under each hoof, the tail a single hook curling to the edge of the paper. The cinnabar was still wet, and in the strokes something like a hair-thin light slid down the horse's legs into the four circles under its hooves and was gone. Xiaoman held it in a long while, and what came out was: "…What the stamping hell kind of talisman is this?" The words were barely out when he saw, in one corner, a line of cinnabar characters no bigger than rice grains: *Hoof-It Charm.* And under it, smaller still: *One stamp underfoot, and off at once.*

The fur on Silver Moon's face stood up in disgust. "One of my hairs, for this. 'Off at once' — off where? Drawn like that — I could draw you a better one myself." The paw went in, and she was asleep again. That one tail dimmed a notch further. It never eats for free; touch it once, and it takes a bite of you.

The talisman — *one stamp underfoot*: stuck on his sole, or stamped under it? And off to where? He couldn't make it out; scrap paper, but she had paid a hair from her tail for it, and he couldn't bring himself to throw it away. He folded it into a small square and tucked it into the pocket inside his belt — his mother had sewn it for coppers, and it had never once held a copper.

He shoved the floor's worth of junk under the woodpile, and at the very end a pill rolled out from under the rice crust: jade green, clear as a drop of frozen dew. There were lines on it; he counted them once, and again: nine, all gold, one next to another round the pill, like a man winding a sash round his waist turn by turn; carved between the lines, two characters no bigger than rice grains: *Spring Return.* He put his nose to it: a beany smell, sweet at the back — that astragalus stalk had bought it.

He knew what one line looked like: his uncle had said the Jishi Hall kept spring-return pills in a glass jar on the counter, dark and dull, one line, a few black spots, five taels apiece. The one in his hand had nine.

exits.means: keeps the pill in a chilli-oil bottle for his father's knee, and keeps the night watch half a month on a broken rib

story.zh:
他把丹托在手心里，肋骨一抽一抽地疼。他知道这东西能做什么：吞下去，今夜断的骨头便接上了，肿便消了，今夜、明夜、往后的每一夜，他都能好好地站在药园里，月底稳稳地过账。马小宝那半句话，就落空了。

他把丹送到嘴边。

怀里那封信硌了他一下。**膝盖比去年重了，阴天下不了炕，晴天照去。**他爹拖着那条腿，一个人过断碑，往黑松岭里走，为的是两只兔子。

炉盖上那只小兽睁着眼睛，看着他。

他把手放了下来。

伙房的胖大娘有一只装辣椒油的小瓷瓶，空了要扔，他去伙房讨了来，在井边洗了七遍，还是一股辣味儿。他把那颗丹装了进去，塞紧，揣进怀里，贴着那封信。

捎是捎不下去的。交给一个光脚孩子，走三天山路——他要是揭开瓶塞闻一闻呢？就算到了家，一个进门一个月、交不起公中的杂灵根，捎回家一颗济世堂一辈子没见过的丹，马三在门框上敲着短棍问：沈老大，你儿子在山上，偷了谁家的？他托那孩子给舅舅捎一句口信：儿好，勿念。叫爹别进黑松岭。又摸出三文钱——他身上统共只有这三文——塞给那光脚的孩子。那孩子捏着三文钱，看了他半天，道：「你舅舅说了，三文钱他给过了。」把钱又塞了回来，挑起担子走了。小满攥着那三文钱，脸上热了半天。

那天夜里，子时，他翻不过墙，照旧从豁口里爬出去，爬到药园，在巡夜簿上十三夜那一格，按了一个手印。

那以后的半个月，沈小满是断着一根肋骨巡的夜。

白天，他照旧去讲堂，照旧挑水，挑一担，歇三回，肩膀不敢换。饭堂里，马小宝天天端着空碗从他桌边经过，天天停一停，拿指头戳那一个地方：「师弟，好些了没有？」戳一下，他眼前白一下，嘴上道：「好些了，师兄。」

每天酉时交班。阿禾扛着锄头从园子里出来，把一天的数报给他：哪一畦抽了新叶，哪一株打了蔫，紫玉参四十一。他夜里再数一遍，卯时把数报还给她。两个人的数，半个月没差过一株。她报数的时候不看他的脸，只看他捂肋骨的那只手；报完了，从袖子里摸出一个煮鸡蛋，搁在园门的石阶上，扛着锄头走了。

夜里，他坐在药园东角阿禾那一圈红线旁边，灵草中间。肋骨疼，一口气吸不到底，他就不吸到底，学那个萝卜筐里的孩子，肚子一鼓，一落，浅浅的，落得长长的。灵草夜里吐出来的那点气，稠得像娘过年熬的那一锅粥，一口一口落下去，肚子底下那一团暖，一夜往下坠一丝；坐得久了，近旁几株灵草的叶子，都朝他这边歪过来，像葵花朝着日头。小狰蹲在他脚边，冲着黑地里，一声不吭。

十五夜里，墙头上「沙」的一响，冒出一个脑袋来。小满没动。那人骑在墙头上，四下里张望，张望到他这里，停住了。

是老蔫。

月亮底下，两个人隔着半个园子，看了很久。一个坐在灵草中间，脸上还青着；一个骑在墙头上，手里攥着一只空布袋。老蔫的嘴动了动，什么也没说出来。他慢慢地，从墙头上退了回去，脚下一滑，墙外「咕咚」一声，接着是一瘸一拐、走远了的脚步。

天亮以后，小满在墙根草里捡到一张油纸，叠成方块，还带着一点甜香，纸角上印着一个红戳——县城那家点心铺子的戳。整个沉鼎观，吃得起这家桂花糕的，只有一个人。他把油纸夹进了巡夜簿里。

十月廿二，天刚亮，柴房的门给人一脚踹开了。马小宝站在门口，身后是周衡，再后头是他的跟班，鞋头补着黑布的那一个也在。通铺那边听见动静，窗口探出来一排脑袋。马小宝一把掀开小狰睡觉的那堆干草——草底下，赫然躺着一株紫玉参，叶子还是鲜的。「药园最值钱的东西。」马小宝道，「畜生就是畜生，改不了偷。巡夜的养贼，周师兄，您怎么记？」

周衡翻开账簿：「紫玉参，月初四十二。」小满道：「我夜夜数，四十一。」马小宝一拍巴掌：「听听！少了一株，巡夜的倒不报！」

小满蹲下去，把那株参拈起来，看它的茬口。十月初九药园西头那株给啃了的灵草，茬口是齐的，却是毛的，一口咬断，牙印一道一道。这一株的茬口，是光的，斜斜的一道，平得像镜子。「师兄，」他把参递给周衡，「狰是拿牙啃的。这一株，是拿刀切的。」

马小宝道：「刀切的？那更好说了。」他转过身，冲着窗口那一排脑袋，嗓门放大了，「叶子还鲜着，昨夜切的。昨夜药园里就一个巡夜的——监守自盗，切了喂畜生，畜生吃不完，藏在窝里。周师兄，这块令牌，该归谁？」

窗口那排脑袋，一齐看小满。小满张了张嘴。昨夜就他一个，这话不假；他那一句「我夜夜数」，这会儿说出来，倒像是替自己圆。

「不是昨夜。」

阿禾不知什么时候站在了门外头，扛着那把小锄头，裤腿上带着露水——她卯时进园子，在园门口望见一行人往柴房来，顺手把巡夜簿从门上摘了下来。她把锄头靠在门框上，翻开小本子，冲周衡道：「周师兄，药园白天归我，我天天数。」她一页一页念，念得平平的，像念别人家的账：「十月初八，酉时，收工，紫玉参四十二。初九，辰时，上工，四十一。初十，四十一。十一，四十一……昨天酉时，四十一。」她把本子转过去给周衡看，「昨夜没少。少的那一株，是初八酉时到初九辰时之间没的。」

周衡道：「初八那一夜，是沈师弟头一夜巡。」

阿禾道：「巡夜簿上，那一格写着两个名字。」她把巡夜簿翻到初八那一格：一个手印，旁边一行大字，墨写得又黑又粗——**马小宝陪巡。子时至丑时。**

柴房里静了一静。马小宝的脸先红，后白，又绿了，脑门上的汗一颗一颗往下掉：「我是去陪他！我们三个，就坐在石阶上——」

阿禾道：「嗯。初九辰时，石阶上丢着一只食盒。」她从本子里抖出一片叶子来，压得扁扁的，紫得发黑，叶脉里一道银线，「盒底一撮湿泥，还有这个。我捡的，夹在本子里，记了一笔。」她拿那片叶子去比周衡手里那株参。参茎上缺了一片叶，断口正对得上。

窗口有人「哦——」地拖了一声长腔，又赶紧捂住了嘴。鞋头补黑布的那个跟班，往人后头缩了半步。小狰从小满脚边钻出来，冲着他抽了两抽鼻子，「咔」地叫了一声。马小宝的嘴张开，又合上，又张开，像一条叫人甩上了岸的鱼——再往下说一句，那一夜提着食盒往园子里头去的是谁，便要一个一个地说出来了。

阿禾却把本子合上了，口气还是平平的：「许是那夜哪位师兄在园子里捡着了，怕丢，替园子收着，今早送回来——送错了窝。」她看着马小宝，「是吧，马师兄？」

马小宝瞪着她，眼珠子都快瞪出眶来了。半晌，从牙缝里挤出一个字：「……是。」

周衡看看阿禾，看看马小宝，把那株参揣进袖子里：「送回来的。账上不记。」抱着账簿走了。马小宝一甩袖子，带着人走了，走过门口，一脚踢翻了门边的水桶，水泼湿了他自己半条裤腿。窗口那排脑袋缩了回去，谁也没说破。

小满等人走远了，才道：「你初九就知道了？」

阿禾道：「知道。」

「那怎么不说？」

「初九说，是告状。今天说，是对账。」她把那片叶子夹回本子里，「他自己把参送上门来，我才有账可对。」

「那你怎么又放他下来？」

阿禾把锄头扛上肩：「拆穿了，他下不来台。他下不来台，他表伯就要下来了。」

月底，还有六天。

到了十月廿五那一夜，他坐在灵草中间，一口气落下去，肚子底下「咚」的一声，那一团暖猛地往下一沉，沉得更深，像一块干了一冬的地，一镢头刨下去，又刨出一层来；刨开了，能盛的，一下子多了一倍。练气二层。

是他一夜一夜，断着一根肋骨，自己坐出来的。

十月廿八，周衡盘月底的账，盘到药园那一页，天已擦黑。小满在执事房门口候着；马小宝也在，身后跟着鞋头补黑布的那个，还有老蔫，站在门槛外头。周衡拿指头点着账簿念：「初十，入账灵兽一只。初十至今日，药园丢——」他抬眼看了看门框上那一位，又低下头，「零。」

小满把巡夜簿里夹着的那张油纸抽出来，放在账簿上：「十五夜里，墙头上来过一个人，看了一眼，回去了。墙根底下，掉了这个。」纸角一个红戳。门槛外头，老蔫的脸一下子白了。小满没有看他。

马小宝道：「一张油纸，谁知道是哪儿捡的？」他一步跨进门来，指着小满，「零？那是他自己吃了！周师兄，一个漏勺，进门一个月，夜夜坐在灵草堆里，草叶子都往他身上歪——偷了灵草吃，吃出一层来！」

小满道：「师兄怎么知道，草叶子往我身上歪？」

执事房里静了下来。马小宝张着嘴，看看周衡，看看房梁，半天才缓过一口气来，声音反倒高了：「……你请人验！请褚先生来，看他是一层，还是二层！」

这一句，是真刀子。一个漏勺，一个半月二层——这话要是传开了，不用马小宝再说一个字，全外门都会替他往下想。

小满没去看马小宝。他对周衡道：「师兄，请褚先生来验。」

褚先生是给人从讲堂里请过来的，山羊胡子一翘一翘，很不耐烦。他也不多话，一把扣住小满的手腕。一股凉丝丝的气，从他腕子上钻了进来，顺着经脉，一路往里探。小满闭上眼睛，不躲，也不压，由它探。褚先生那股气探进来，碰到哪里，哪里便像给铁刷子刷了一下；碰着肋骨，疼得他眼前发白。

褚先生探了足有一盏茶的工夫，才松了手，眉头一皱：「二层。」马小宝一拍巴掌：「我说什么来着！」褚先生不理他，又按了按小满的肋骨，按到左边那一根，手停住了。小满没出声，额头上的汗一颗一颗往下掉。

「这根骨头，还断着。」褚先生道，「半个月了。」他转过身，冲马小宝道，「药园的灵草，治伤最灵。他要是偷吃了一株，这根骨头早长上了。」周衡把巡夜簿翻开，推到他跟前，一夜一个手印，从初十起，一夜也不缺。褚先生翻了两页，道：「灵草堆里，灵气厚。漏勺坐在那里头，漏一半，也存下一半。坐了半个月，坐出一层来——」他哼了一声，「漏勺还是漏勺。」

马小宝一口桂花糕正咽到一半，呛在了喉咙里，咳得弯下腰去，也没咳出一句话来。

褚先生走到门口，又停住，回过头来，多看了小满一眼，看他捂着肋骨的那只手，到底什么也没问，走了。

周衡把巡夜簿合上，压在账簿底下，道：「只认账，不认脸。药园巡夜，沈小满。工钱，残株，月一篮。」从桌子底下拎出一只竹篮来，篮里是这个月拔下来的残株：虫咬的，长歪的，灵气散了一半的，堆了小半篮。

小满拎着篮子走出执事房，扶着墙站了一会儿——褚先生那一盏茶的铁刷子，刷得他肋下一阵一阵地疼。怀里那只辣椒油瓶，隔着衣裳，硌着那根没长好的骨头。

那天夜里，外门后院的井台边上，马小宝一个人蹲着，拿井水洗下巴。他是三灵根、色浊，他爹等不得，一个月里硬喂了他三瓶聚气丹，喂出了一个练气一层，也喂出了下巴上三个小黑点。他拿皂角搓，拿井台上的粗砂磨，磨得下巴通红，那三个黑点还在。他从怀里摸出装聚气丹的瓷瓶，倒过来，往手心里磕。磕出来三颗，是这个月剩下的最后三颗，一道纹，纹边上一圈黑点，跟他下巴上的一模一样。

他想起去年秋天在沈家门口，叫沈小满学狗叫，沈小满说「正在学」，他笑了好几天；如今想起来，一点也不好笑了。他想起沈小满那根断着的骨头，想起周衡账簿上那张油纸，想起腊月那一颗筑基丹。讲堂里说起沈小满，说的是「那个收狰的」，不是「那个漏勺」。他想：他凭什么？他又想：他吃一口，我吃三口。

他把那三颗丹，一口吞了下去，连水都没喝，干咽，咽得脖子一伸一伸的。那股暖升上来了，热烘烘的，烧得他满脸通红，烧得下巴上那三个黑点一跳一跳地疼。他咬着牙，指甲抠进井台的石缝里，等它过去。他站起身来，擦了擦嘴，从袖子里又摸出一块桂花糕，咬了一口。还是饿。

第二天一早，外门的告示栏上，贴出了一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：

**沉鼎秘境，十年一开。冬月初一，练气弟子，内外门皆可入。**
story.en:
He held the pill in his palm, his ribs throbbing. He knew what it could do: swallow it, and tonight the broken bone would knit and the swelling go down; tonight, tomorrow night, every night after, he could stand properly in the herb garden and pass the month-end accounts without a wobble. Ma Xiaobao's half-sentence would come to nothing.

He lifted the pill to his mouth.

The letter in his coat dug into him. **His knee is worse than last year — on overcast days he can't get off the kang, and on clear days he goes anyway.** His father dragging that leg past the broken stele alone, into the Heisong Ridge, for the sake of two rabbits.

The little beast on the lid had its eyes open, watching him.

He lowered his hand.

The fat auntie in the kitchen had a little porcelain chilli-oil bottle, empty and about to be thrown out; he went to the kitchen and begged it, and washed it seven times at the well, and it still smelled of chilli. He put the pill in, stoppered it tight, and tucked it into his coat against the letter.

Send it down he could not. Hand it to a barefoot boy for three days of mountain road — and what if he pulled the stopper and had a sniff? And even if it got home: a mixed root a month through the gate, who couldn't even pay the common fund, sending home a pill the Jishi Hall had never seen in its life — Ma San would rap his short club on the doorframe and ask: Shen the Elder, your son up the mountain — whose did he steal? He gave the boy a message for his uncle: Your son is well, don't worry. Tell Dad not to go into the Heisong Ridge. Then he took out three coppers — all he had on him — and pushed them at the barefoot boy. The boy held the coppers and looked at him a long time. "Your uncle said he's paid me the three coppers already." He pushed them back, shouldered his load, and left. Xiaoman stood holding the three coppers, his face hot for a long while.

That night at midnight, unable to climb the wall, he crawled out through the drain gap as before, crawled to the herb garden, and pressed a handprint into the box for the thirteenth night in the watch book.

For the half-month after that, Shen Xiaoman kept the night watch with a broken rib.

By day he went to lectures as usual and carried water as usual — one load, three rests, never daring to change shoulders. In the refectory Ma Xiaobao passed his table every day with an empty bowl, stopped every day, and poked that one spot: "Brother, any better?" At each poke his sight went white, and his mouth said, "Better, senior brother."

They changed over at dusk each day. Ah He came out of the garden with her hoe on her shoulder and gave him the day's count: which bed had put out new leaves, which plant was wilting, forty-one purple jade ginseng. He counted again in the night, and at the hour of mao gave the count back to her. In half a month their two counts never differed by one plant. While she gave the count she didn't look at his face, only at the hand he held to his rib; when she had finished she took a boiled egg from her sleeve, set it on the step by the garden gate, shouldered her hoe and left.

By night he sat in the east corner of the garden beside Ah He's ring of red thread, among the herbs. His rib hurt and a breath wouldn't go all the way down, so he didn't take it all the way down; he did as the baby in the radish basket did, belly rising, falling, shallow, the fall long. The breath the herbs gave off at night was as thick as the pot his mother cooked at New Year, and breath after breath went down, and the warmth beneath his belly sank a hair each night; when he had sat a long while, the leaves of the nearest herbs all leaned his way, like sunflowers turning to the sun. Little Zheng squatted at his feet facing the dark, without a sound.

On the night of the fifteenth there was a rustle on top of the wall, and a head came up. Xiaoman didn't move. The figure sat astride the wall, looking all round, and when its look came round to him it stopped.

It was Laonian.

Under the moon the two of them looked at each other across half the garden for a long time — one sitting among the herbs, his face still bruised; one astride the wall, an empty cloth bag in his fist. Laonian's lips moved; nothing came out. Slowly he backed down off the wall; his foot slipped, there was a *thud* outside, then limping footsteps going away.

After dawn Xiaoman found a sheet of oiled paper in the grass at the foot of the wall, folded square, still faintly sweet, with a red stamp on the corner — the stamp of that pastry shop in the county town. In all of Chending Temple only one person could afford that shop's osmanthus cake. He slipped the paper into the watch book.

The twenty-second of the tenth month, at first light, someone kicked the woodshed door open. Ma Xiaobao stood in the doorway; behind him Zhou Heng, and behind him again his followers — the one with the black patch on his shoe among them. Over at the dormitory, at the noise, a row of heads came out of the window. Ma Xiaobao flung aside the heap of straw where Little Zheng slept — and under it, plain as day, lay a purple jade ginseng, its leaves still fresh. "The most valuable thing in the herb garden," said Ma Xiaobao. "A beast is a beast — it can't stop stealing. The watchman keeping the thief — Brother Zhou, how will you write that down?"

Zhou Heng opened his ledger. "Purple jade ginseng: forty-two at the start of the month." Xiaoman said, "I count them every night. Forty-one." Ma Xiaobao clapped his hands. "Hear that! One gone, and the watchman never reported it!"

Xiaoman crouched, picked the ginseng up, and looked at the cut. The herb gnawed at the west end of the garden on the ninth of the tenth month had a clean stump, but a ragged one — bitten off at one go, tooth marks in rows. This one's stump was smooth: one slanting stroke, flat as a mirror. "Senior Brother," he said, handing the ginseng to Zhou Heng, "a zheng gnaws with its teeth. This one was cut with a knife."

"With a knife? Easier still," said Ma Xiaobao. He turned to the row of heads at the window and raised his voice. "The leaves are still fresh — cut last night. Last night there was one watchman in the herb garden. Robbing what he's set to guard, cutting it to feed his beast, and the beast couldn't finish it and hid it in its nest. Brother Zhou, whose should the tag be?"

The row of heads at the window all looked at Xiaoman. Xiaoman opened his mouth. Last night it was only him, that much was true; and "I count them every night", said now, would sound like covering for himself.

"Not last night."

Ah He was standing outside the door, who knew since when, her little hoe on her shoulder, dew on her trouser legs — she went into the garden at the hour of mao, had seen from the gate a party heading for the woodshed, and had lifted the watch book off the gate on her way. She leaned the hoe on the doorframe, opened her notebook, and said to Zhou Heng, "Brother Zhou, the herb garden is mine by day. I count every day." She read page after page, flat and even, as if reading someone else's accounts: "Eighth of the tenth, evening, end of work: purple jade ginseng, forty-two. Ninth, hour of chen, start of work: forty-one. Tenth, forty-one. Eleventh, forty-one… Yesterday evening: forty-one." She turned the book round for Zhou Heng to see. "Nothing went last night. The one that's missing went between the evening of the eighth and the hour of chen on the ninth."

"The night of the eighth," said Zhou Heng, "was Brother Shen's first night on watch."

"In the watch book," said Ah He, "that box has two names in it." She turned the watch book to the box for the eighth: one handprint, and beside it a line in big characters, the ink black and thick — **Ma Xiaobao kept watch with him. Hour of Zi to hour of Chou.**

The woodshed went quiet. Ma Xiaobao's face went red first, then white, then green, sweat rolling down his forehead bead by bead. "I was keeping him company! The three of us sat on the steps the whole —"

"Mm," said Ah He. "At the hour of chen on the ninth, a food box was left lying on the steps." From her notebook she shook out a leaf, pressed flat, purple almost to black, a silver thread in its veins. "A pinch of wet earth in the bottom, and this. I picked it up, kept it in the book, made a note." She held the leaf against the ginseng in Zhou Heng's hand. One leaf was missing from the stem, and the break matched.

At the window someone went "Ohhh —", dragging it out long, and quickly clapped a hand over his mouth. The follower with the black patch on his shoe edged half a step back behind the others. Little Zheng slipped out from by Xiaoman's feet, sniffed twice towards him, and went *crack*. Ma Xiaobao's mouth opened, and shut, and opened again, like a fish flung up on the bank — one more word, and who had carried a food box off into the garden that night would have to be said, name by name.

But Ah He shut her notebook, her voice as flat as before. "Perhaps one of the senior brothers found it in the garden that night, and kept it safe for the garden in case it got lost, and brought it back this morning — to the wrong nest." She looked at Ma Xiaobao. "Isn't that so, Brother Ma?"

Ma Xiaobao glared at her till his eyes nearly popped from their sockets. At last he squeezed one word through his teeth: "…Yes."

Zhou Heng looked at Ah He, looked at Ma Xiaobao, and tucked the ginseng into his sleeve. "Returned. It doesn't go in the books." He took his ledger and left. Ma Xiaobao flung his sleeve and left with his men, kicking over the water bucket by the door as he passed and soaking half of his own trouser leg. The row of heads drew back from the window, and nobody said what everyone knew.

When they had gone a good way, Xiaoman said, "You knew on the ninth?"

"I knew," said Ah He.

"Then why didn't you say?"

"Said on the ninth, it's telling tales. Said today, it's checking the books." She slipped the leaf back into her notebook. "He brought the ginseng to the door himself. Only then did I have books to check."

"Then why let him down off the hook?"

Ah He shouldered her hoe. "Show him up, and he can't climb down. If he can't climb down, his uncle comes down instead."

Six days left to the month's end.

On the night of the twenty-fifth of the tenth month, sitting among the herbs, he let a breath fall, and beneath his belly something went *dong*; the warmth sank suddenly, deeper, like ground dried out all winter when a mattock bites in and turns up another layer; once turned, it could hold twice as much at a stroke. The second level of qi refining.

He had sat it out himself, night after night, with a broken rib.

On the twenty-eighth of the tenth month Zhou Heng did the month-end reckoning; by the time he reached the herb garden's page it was already getting dark. Xiaoman waited at the steward's office door; Ma Xiaobao was there too, with the one with the black-patched shoe behind him, and Laonian, standing outside the threshold. Zhou Heng read off the ledger, his finger on it: "The tenth: entered, one spirit beast. From the tenth to today, the herb garden has lost —" he raised his eyes to the one in the doorframe, then lowered them again, "— none."

Xiaoman drew out the oiled paper tucked in the watch book and laid it on the ledger. "On the night of the fifteenth someone came up on the wall, had a look, and went back. At the foot of the wall, this was dropped." A red stamp on the corner. Outside the threshold, Laonian's face went white at once. Xiaoman did not look at him.

Ma Xiaobao said, "A bit of oiled paper — who knows where he picked it up?" He stepped in over the threshold and pointed at Xiaoman. "None? Because he ate them himself! Brother Zhou — a skimmer, a month through the gate, sitting night after night in the herb beds, the leaves all leaning his way — he stole herbs and ate himself up a level!"

Xiaoman said, "How does Senior Brother know the leaves lean my way?"

The steward's office went quiet. Ma Xiaobao stood open-mouthed, looked at Zhou Heng, looked at the rafters, and only after a long while got his breath back — and his voice came out higher: "…Get someone to test him! Fetch Master Chu — see if he's the first level or the second!"

That was a real knife. A skimmer, the second level in a month and a half — once that got about, Ma Xiaobao wouldn't need to say another word; the whole outer court would do the rest of the thinking for him.

Xiaoman didn't look at Ma Xiaobao. He said to Zhou Heng, "Senior Brother, please send for Master Chu to test me."

Master Chu had been fetched from the lecture hall, his goat's beard jerking, very impatient. He wasted no words; he clamped Xiaoman's wrist. A thread of cool qi bored in at his wrist and probed inward along the meridians. Xiaoman closed his eyes; he neither dodged nor pressed it down, and let it probe. Wherever Master Chu's qi touched as it probed, it was as if a wire brush had scraped him; when it reached the rib, the pain whitened his sight.

Master Chu probed a good while, the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, before he let go, frowning: "Layer two." Ma Xiaobao clapped his hands: "What did I tell you!" Chu paid him no attention. He pressed Xiaoman's ribs too, and at the one on the left his hand stopped. Xiaoman made no sound; the sweat dropped from his forehead bead by bead.

"This bone is still broken," said Master Chu. "Half a month now." He turned to Ma Xiaobao. "The herb garden's herbs are the best thing there is for healing. If he'd stolen and eaten even one, this bone would have knit long ago." Zhou Heng opened the night-watch book and pushed it across to him: a handprint a night, from the tenth on, not one night missing. Chu turned two pages. "Among the herbs the qi is thick. A skimmer sitting in the middle of it leaks half and still keeps half. Half a month of sitting, and he's sat himself up a layer —" he snorted, "a skimmer is still a skimmer."

Ma Xiaobao had half swallowed a mouthful of osmanthus cake; it caught in his throat, and he doubled over coughing, and coughed up not a single word.

At the door Master Chu stopped again and looked back, one more look at Xiaoman — at the hand clutching his ribs — and in the end asked nothing, and left.

Zhou Heng closed the watch book and put it under the ledger. "I go by the accounts, not by faces. Herb garden night watch, Shen Xiaoman. Wages, culls, one basket a month." From under the table he lifted a bamboo basket; in it were this month's culls — the insect-bitten, the crooked, the ones with half their qi gone — a small half-basket of them.

Xiaoman carried the basket out of the steward's office and stood a while with a hand on the wall — a teacup's time of Master Chu's wire brush had left his side aching in waves. The chilli-oil bottle in his coat pressed, through the cloth, against the bone that had not knit.

That night, by the well platform in the outer court's back yard, Ma Xiaobao crouched alone, washing his chin with well water. He had three roots, and murky ones; his father couldn't wait, and in one month had force-fed him three bottles of qi-gathering pills, feeding him up to Qi Refining level one — and three little black spots on his chin. He scrubbed it with soap-pod, ground it with the coarse grit on the well's edge till it was red raw, and the three black spots were still there. He took the porcelain bottle of qi-gathering pills from his coat, turned it upside down, and knocked it against his palm. Three came out — the last three left this month — one line, a ring of black spots round the line, exactly like the ones on his chin.

He thought of last autumn at the Shens' door, making Shen Xiaoman bark like a dog, and Shen Xiaoman saying "I'm learning" — he'd laughed for days; thinking of it now, it wasn't funny at all. He thought of Shen Xiaoman's broken bone, of the oiled paper in Zhou Heng's ledger, of the twelfth month's one foundation pill. In the lecture hall when they spoke of Shen Xiaoman, they said "the one who caught the zheng", not "the skimmer". He thought: what makes him so special? Then he thought: he takes one mouthful, I take three.

He swallowed the three pills at one go, without even water — dry, his neck stretching and stretching with it. The warmth came up, hot, burning his face red, setting the three black spots on his chin throbbing. He set his teeth and dug his nails into the cracks of the well stones, waiting for it to pass. He stood up, wiped his mouth, took another osmanthus cake from his sleeve, and bit into it. Still hungry.

Early the next morning a new notice went up on the outer court's notice board, the ink not yet dry:

**The Chending hidden realm opens once in ten years. The first of the eleventh month — all Qi Refining disciples, inner court and outer, may enter.**
